builder_plan.scenario: You already need task-specific training and want to reduce its memory or compute cost.
builder_plan.change: Change only the training technique on a small controlled run after checking prerequisites.
builder_plan.baseline: Your current training recipe with the same model, data split, and evaluation.
steps: Locate the paper's implementation and check its license, model support, data needs, and hardware requirements. Stop here if you cannot obtain the required artifacts.
Save a small set of representative product tasks and expected outcomes. Keep evaluation tasks out of any training or tuning, and choose quality and cost limits before running.
Run the baseline and the proposed change on identical inputs. Keep other settings fixed and repeat paired runs to expose variation.
Save per-task outputs, failures, timings, and all usage costs. Review regressions before expanding the test.
builder_plan.measure: Held-out quality, peak memory, training time, and full compute cost to the target quality.
builder_plan.decision: Keep the change only if it meets your preselected quality and latency limits and improves the metric you care about after setup and operating costs. Otherwise retain the baseline. This is an exploration plan, not a validated recommendation.

title: Mixture of Latent Recursions for Low-Rank Adaptation
summary: MoLR replaces the fixed low-rank LoRA update with recursive refinement of the down-projected latent using a shared transformation, plus a threshold-based router that assigns each token a recursion depth. It costs a small latency increase from iterative latent computation and added routing complexity, with only negligible parameter overhead over LoRA, and offers a tunable inference-time compute-performance trade-off. Failure modes include router imbalance or threshold miscalibration (the paper relies on dynamically adjusted thresholds to prevent collapse to a single depth), latency-sensitive workloads where recursion overhead outweighs quality gains, and the risk that gains do not transfer from the paper's benchmarks to the reader's tasks.
rationale: MoLR is a drop-in LoRA variant runnable on a single 24 GB GPU, but the claimed gains are unquantified in the abstract and the code is not yet released, so it warrants a small-scale pilot against standard LoRA on the team's own tasks rather than immediate adoption.

It costs a small latency increase from iterative latent computation and added routing complexity, with only negligible parameter overhead over LoRA, and offers a tunable inference-time compute-performance trade-off. Failure modes include router imbalance or threshold miscalibration (the paper relies on dynamically adjusted thresholds to prevent collapse to a single depth), latency-sensitive workloads where recursion overhead outweighs quality gains, and the risk that gains do not transfer from the paper's benchmarks to the reader's tasks.

Abstract reports MoLR 'consistently outperforms representative LoRA variants' across language and vision tasks with 'negligible parameter overhead,' but gives no numbers; quantified claims would require the full paper.
